37 In the circuit shown, the ammeter reading is zero.

What is the resistance of resistor R?
A
100 Ω
B
200 Ω
C
400 Ω

hints: Notice the middle wire joins the two divider junctions and the ammeter joins the two bottom wires, so compare the voltage from middle to bottom on each side.
On the left, the $12 \, \text{V}$ is split across $50 \, \Omega$ and $100 \, \Omega$ in series, so calculate the p.d. across the $100 \, \Omega$ resistor.
On the right, the same middle-to-bottom p.d. must appear across the $200 \, \Omega$ resistor from the $24 \, \text{V}$ supply, so use the potential divider ratio with $R$ to solve for $R$.
walkthrough: Take the common bottom wire as reference and call the common middle junction $V_m$. Zero ammeter current means each side keeps its own series current with no cross-flow.

Left side: $12 \, \text{V}$ across $50 \, \Omega + 100 \, \Omega$. By the potential divider, p.d. across the lower $100 \, \Omega$ resistor is $V_m = 12 \times 100/(50+100) = 12 \times 100/150 = 8 \, \text{V}$.

Right side: $24 \, \text{V}$ across $R + 200 \, \Omega$. The p.d. across the lower $200 \, \Omega$ resistor must also be $8 \, \text{V}$ for the two middle points and two bottom points to be at the same potentials.

A.explanation: A $100 \, \Omega$ resistor would make the right divider ratio $1:2$, giving a different middle-to-bottom voltage from the $12 \, \text{V}$ left side.

B.explanation: A $200 \, \Omega$ resistor would split the $24 \, \text{V}$ equally, giving $12 \, \text{V}$ across the $200 \, \Omega$ resistor, not the $8 \, \text{V}$ required for balance.

C.explanation: With $R = 400 \, \Omega$ the p.d. across the $200 \, \Omega$ resistor is $8 \, \text{V}$, matching the $8 \, \text{V}$ across the $100 \, \Omega$ resistor, so no current flows in the ammeter branch.

D.explanation: A $600 \, \Omega$ resistor would make the voltage across the $200 \, \Omega$ resistor only $6 \, \text{V}$, which is less than the left-side $8 \, \text{V}$ and would drive a current through the ammeter.
